content:
* A Russian bomb attack on Kharkiv struck a residential building and a playground, killing seven people and injuring at least 77, local authorities said. The death toll rose to seven after rescuers recovered a woman’s body from the rubble, and a 14-year-old girl was among those confirmed dead, President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said. About 20 of the wounded were reported in severe condition by regional governor Oleh Syniehubov, who described frantic rescue work amid collapsing concrete and twisted metal. Emergency teams worked against the clock to search apartments and clear blockages while neighbours and volunteers assisted with first aid.

* Ukrainian officials said five aerial guided glide bombs were launched from planes flying out of Russia’s Belgorod region, and they called for the ability to strike Russian airbases to prevent similar strikes. Zelenskiy renewed appeals to western partners, arguing there was no rational reason to restrict Ukraine’s defences and stressing that a strike like this might have been prevented with longer-range weapons. He said control of the skies was essential to protect towns near the border and that denying certain weapon systems left civilians exposed. Diplomats in Kyiv and partner capitals were briefed on the incident as discussions continued about what medium of support would most effectively reduce civilian casualties.

* Russian regional officials responded by accusing Ukraine of firing cluster munitions into Belgorod and surrounding suburbs, reporting at least five dead and 37 wounded, including children. Vyacheslav Gladkov, the regional governor, said one woman and four men died before ambulances could reach them, and he posted video showing a house on fire and rescue crews at the scene. The exchange of claims between Kyiv and Moscow added to the confusion about who targeted which populated areas and when, complicating independent verification on the ground. International monitors and journalists struggled with limited access to the border regions as both sides disputed details.

* Hospitals in Kharkiv and nearby towns reported receiving dozens of wounded people, and staff said they were operating under pressure but managed to stabilize many of the injured. Mobile phone reception in parts of the city was intermittent after the strikes, affecting relatives trying to locate loved ones and hampering coordination for volunteer groups. A communications tower near the strike zone sustained damage, further disrupting calls and internet access for hours during rescue operations. Authorities appealed for calm and urged residents to rely on official channels for verified information while repair crews worked to restore services.

* Local and international aid organizations mobilized to provide medical supplies, psychological support and emergency shelter for those displaced by the bombing, and volunteers set up collection points for clothing and food. Investigations by Ukrainian and independent sources were expected to follow, aiming to document the weapons used and the sequence of events leading to casualties in civilian areas. The incident renewed debates in foreign capitals about the scope and type of military assistance Kyiv needs, with some allies cautious about escalation while others emphasized the need for greater defensive reach. Meanwhile, families of the victims mourned losses and sought information in the midst of ongoing uncertainty and fear.
